65 1 CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 1.1 Research Background and Motivation The global retail industry is undergoing a structural transformation driven by e - commerce. Projections indicate that the annual value of global retail e -commerce will grow to $6.42 trillion by 2025, accounting for over 20% of total retail sales [1].

To cop e with the new normal of e -commerce orders —characterized by small batches, high frequency, and time sensitivity—traditional warehousing models are no longer adequate, prompting widespread adoption of Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). In an RMFS, hundreds of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) work collaboratively within a grid-based warehouse, capable of increasing order picking efficiency severalfold. However, high -density AMR operations have given rise to new operational bottlenecks. Traffic congestion at intersections, waiting delays between robots, and frequent acceleration and deceleration behaviors not only directly limit the system’s overall throughput but also significantly increase energy consumption and carbon emissions. This issue has become critically important under the increasingly stringent global policies on sustainable development and carbon neutrality: • Significant Carbon Footprint : Carbon emissions from transportation and warehousing activities account for approximately 24% of total global greenhouse gas emissions and are considered a priority area for carbon reduction by international logistics leaders like DHL [2].

2 • Urgent Policy Pressure : The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), initiated in 2023 and set to take full effect in 2026, will impose costs on high -carbon-intensity imported products. This will compel businesses throughout the supply chain to rigorously scrutinize and manage carbon emissions in their warehousing and transportation links [3].

Against this backdrop, academia has begun applying intelligent methods like Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize RMFS operations. Some studies have used deep reinforcement learning for order scheduling to minimize costs [4], while others have reduced total energy consumption by about 3–5% by adjusting traffic strategies and robot speeds [5].

However, these studies either focus on order -level scheduling or leave room for exploration in the trade -off between energy consumption and efficiency. More specifically, there is still a lack of a control framework focused at the intersection level that aims to achieve the dual optimization goals of “energy -efficiency” at a micro-level by reducing unnecessary waiting and frequent “stop-and-go” behaviors.

To fill this research gap, this study employs Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to design an intersection controller. This method combines the global search capabilities of evolutionary algorithms with the real -time decision -making advantages of deep reinforcement learning. It aims to provide an “adaptive, energy-aware” right-of-way allocation mechanism for RMFS intersections, with the expectation of effectively reducing the energy consumption per task for AMRs while maintaining order processing efficiency. This is a direct technical approach to addressing the challenge of a high carbon footprint. 3 1.2 Research Objectives The core objective of this study is to investigate and quantify the trade -off relationship between two conflicting goals —system throughput and energy efficiency—for different control strategies addressing traffic congestion in Robotic Mobile Fulfillment Systems (RMFS). The specific objectives are threefold: 1.

Since Kiva Systems was acquired by Amazon and deployed on a massive scale [7], RMFS has become a cornerstone of modern e-commerce logistics.

chunks.text: Studies show that its productivity can be two to four times that of traditional 7 warehouses. As the number of robots deployed by companies like Amazon exceeds 750,000, the operational density and complexity of these systems have reached unprecedented levels [8]. However, high -density deployment brings a new and severe bottleneck: Traffic Congestion.

chunks.text: As defined in Chapter 3 of this study, when a large number of robots perform tasks within a limited aisle network, especially at intersections, conflicts and waiting periods easily arise from improper right-of-way coordination [9]. This triggers a series of cascading negative effects, not only causing delays in order fulfillment and reducing overall system throughput but also, as recent research indicates, the frequent stop-and-go behavior significantly increases overall energy consumption [10] and may accelerate robot battery aging, thereby increasing operational costs.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: Therefore, designing an intersection management strategy that is adaptive and considers both efficiency and energy sustainability has become a core challenge in enhancing the overall performance of RMFS. In the complex decision-making framework of RMFS, traffic control and path planning are the most critical elements related to real-time system performance. In recent years, much research has been dedicated to solving this problem. For example, one study proposed [11] proposed a path planning method combining the A* algorithm with DQN, while another study used [12] used an attention -based DRL model to collaboratively handle multi -AGV scheduling and shelf reconfiguration. These studies highlight the immense potential of intelligent algorithms in RMFS operational optimization.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: Although this study focuses on intersection traffic control, its optimization goals —improving system fluidity and efficiency—are fundamentally aligned with these research efforts. 8 2.3 Review and Analysis of Intersection Traffic Control Methods To address the problem of intersection traffic in RMFS, various control strategies have been proposed by academia and industry.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: Their development can be broadly categorized into heuristic methods and learning -based methods, reflecting a trend from static rules to dynamic, adaptive control. 2.3.1 Heuristic and Rule-based Controllers Early solutions often relied on manually designed heuristic rules. Their advantages include simple implementation and low computational overhead, making them common baselines for evaluating the performance of more complex algorithms.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: One category is Static Time-based Control, which borrows from traditional urban traffic signal systems by setting fixed cycles for switching right -of-way at intersections. This approach is conceptually similar to early rule-based urban traffic solutions [13] and corresponds to the TimeBasedController designed in Section 3.3.1 of this study.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: However, its fundamental flaw is its complete inability to adapt to real -time traffic flow changes. When traffic fluctuates dramatically, this static strategy is prone to wasting green light time on idle directions or causing unnecessary queue build-up in busy directions. To overcome the shortcomings of static methods, another category, Dynamic Reactive Control, emerged.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: These methods react to the real-time state of the intersection (e.g., queue length). For instance, the work in assigned agent [14] assigned agents to intersections to manage traffic flow based on the priority of incoming robots. Although more flexible, the design of these heuristic rules is highly dependent on expert experience 9 and prior knowledge.

chunks.section: 3. Analyze and Elucidate Performance Trade -off Characteristics: Through in -
chunks.text: Their predefined weights and logic struggle to capture the optimal coordination strategy in complex traffic patterns, often leading to sub -optimal performance in highly dynamic and non-linear traffic scenarios [15]. 2.3.2 Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based Controllers To overcome the limitations of manual rules, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been widely applied to traffic control problems. DRL enables an agent (the controller) to autonomously learn complex decision -making policies through interaction with the environment to maximize long-term cumulative rewards [16]. This paradigm has achieved great success in the macroscopic field of urban traffic signal control. Numerous studies have demonstrated that methods based on Deep Q - Networks (DQN) and its variants significantly outperform traditional methods in reducing vehicle delays and improving network throughput [17].

[19] compared the performance of PPO and DQN in single -intersection control; and Angela et al. [20] designed a reward function that incorporates multi -dimensional information such as pressure, queue, and speed to train DQN agents. These studies fully demonstrate the powerful capabilities of DRL in handling sequential decision-making problems. In recent years, researchers have begun to transfer this paradigm to RMFS scenarios. They typically use local traffic information at intersections (e.g., queue length, waiting time) as the State, switching traffic phases as the Action, and maximizing throughput or minimizing waiting time as the Reward to train the controller [21] [22].

Reward Design Sensitivity: The performance of DQN is highly dependent on dense 10 and well-designed immediate reward signals. However, in complex trade-off problems like the one in this study, designing a perfect immediate reward is extremely difficult. A poorly designed or overly simplified reward function can lead the agent to learn unintended, sub-optimal behaviors (e.g., frequent signal flickering to gain switching rewards) as also noted in recent RL-based signal-control studies. [31] [33] 2. Risk of Local Optima: In complex, high-dimensional state spaces, gradient-based optimization methods can sometimes converge to a local optimum, failing to discover the globally optimal coordination strategy. [34] 3.

chunks.text: Unlike DQN, which attempts to learn a value function, NERL searches directly in the parameter space of the policy network. It treats the weights of a neural network as an individual’s “genes” and uses evolutionary algorithms (such as elitism, crossover, and mutation) to optimize an entire population of agents, ultimately yielding a high - performance control policy [23]. NERL exhibits several unique advantages in solving complex control problems, making it particularly suitable for the objectives of this study: 1.

chunks.section: 1. Robustness to Reward Functions : Evolutionary algorithms are gradient -free,
chunks.text: Robustness to Reward Functions : Evolutionary algorithms are gradient -free, black-box optimization methods that do not require the reward function to be continuous or differentiable. This makes them naturally applicable to handling sparse, delayed, or global performance -based reward signals . For example, the “total number of completed orders” or “total energy consumption” over an entire simulation episode can be directly used as the fitness function. This aligns well with the Global Reward concept designed in Section 3.4.4 of this study, thus avoiding tedious Reward Engineering. 2.

chunks.text: Stronger Global Exploration: The crossover and mutation operations in the evolutionary process facilitate broader exploration in the parameter space. By maintaining population diversity, the risk of getting stuck in local optima is reduced, making it more likely to discover innovative and efficient control strategies. 3. Inherent Parallelism: The evaluation of each individual (policy network) in the population is independent and can be deployed in parallel on multi -core CPUs or computing clusters. This allows for effective use of modern computing resources, 12 significantly reducing the wall-clock time for training [24].

Order and Task Flow The driving force of the simulation comes from orders.

chunks.section: 3. Order and Task Flow
chunks.text: An Order represents a customer’s request and contains multiple SKUs to be picked. The system breaks down an order into one or more Jobs. The core of a job is “transporting a specified pod to a specified workstation,” which is the smallest work unit that can be directly assigned to a robot. The entire process is as follows: 1. The system receives an order. 2. The SKUs required for the order are located on specific pods. 3. The system generates one or more jobs and places them in the job queue. 4. An idle robot takes a job from the queue and begins its work cycle of picking up, delivering, and returning the pod. 5. When all SKUs for an order have been successfully delivered to the workstation, the order is marked as complete. 4. The core of this architecture is to separate the “decision - making algorithm” from the “system execution framework,” ensuring that whether it’s a simple rule-based logic or a complex deep reinforcement learning model, it can operate and be evaluated on th e same foundation. The system is mainly composed of the following three components: 1. TrafficController (Abstract Base Class for Traffic Controllers) This Abstract Base Class (ABC) defines a unified interface that all traffic control strategies must adhere to. Its core method is get_direction(intersection, tick, warehouse), which receives the current detailed state of the intersection (local informatio n) and the 23 state of the entire warehouse system (global information), and returns a traffic decision for that intersection (e.g., "Horizontal" or "Vertical"). By forcing all controllers to implement this interface, the system ensures consistency in how different algorithms are called. Additionally, the base class integrates standardized statistical data collection functions to record various performance metrics. 2.

chunks.section: 2. TrafficControllerFactory (Controller Factory)
chunks.text: TrafficControllerFactory (Controller Factory) This class uses the factory design pattern and is responsible for dynamically creating instances of TrafficController subclasses based on external configurations (such as the controller type specified in the experiment configuration file). When the simulation core needs a controller, it only needs to provide a string identifier like "dqn", "nerl", or "time_based", and the factory will return a corresponding, initialized controller object. This design completely decouples the “creation logic” from the “usag e logic” of the controllers, greatly enhancing the flexibility and scalability of the experimental process, allowing for switching between different control strategies without modifying any core simulation code. 3. IntersectionManager (Intersection Manager) The IntersectionManager is the central coordinator and execution engine of the entire traffic control system. Its operational flow forms a complete closed -loop control system: 1. Holds Controller Instance : During the simulation initialization phase, the IntersectionManager obtains the required controller instance for the current experiment through the controller factory. 2. Drives Decision Loop : In each time unit (tick) of the simulation, the manager 24 iterates through all intersections in the warehouse. 3. Gets Decision : For each intersection, it calls the get_direction() method of the TrafficController instance to get the traffic command for that intersection. 4. Executes Decision : Based on the command returned by the controller, the IntersectionManager updates the internal state of the intersection, such as changing the allowed direction of passage. 5.

These baseline strategies provide a performance reference point, allowing us to quantify the actual improvements brought by the complex algorithm. This study selects two distinct control philosophies as baselines: a Time-Based Strategy representing traditional static centralized management, and a No- Control Strategy representing fully decentralized decision-making.

chunks.section: 3. Energy Consumption Calculation Model
chunks.text: 3.3.1 Time-Based Controller The TimeBasedController is the most basic static traffic control strategy. Its core idea is derived from traditional urban traffic signal systems, completely ignoring real - time traffic flow or any dynamic changes at the intersection. It relies solely on a pre-set, fixed time cycle to switch the right -of-way between horizontal and vertical directions. The advantage of this method is its extreme simplicity and predictability, but its disadvantage is equally obvious—it cannot adapt to fluctuations in traffic demand, easily causing unnecessary waiting during busy times or wasting passage time during light traffic. Design Principles and Decision Logic The operation of this controller is determined entirely by two core parameters: the green light time for the horizontal direction ( 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛) and the green light time for the vertical direction ( 𝑇𝑉_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛). The sum of these two constitutes a complete signal cycle length (𝑇𝑐𝑦𝑐𝑙𝑒).

chunks.section: 3. Energy Consumption Calculation Model
chunks.text: 34 𝑇𝑐𝑦𝑐𝑙𝑒 = 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 + 𝑇𝑉_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 (3 − 11) At any given time tick in the simulation, the controller determines the current position in the signal cycle (𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠) using a modulo operation: 𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠 = tick mod 𝑇𝑐𝑦𝑐𝑙𝑒 (3 − 12) Based on the value of 𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠, the controller decides the direction of passage. If 𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠 is less than the horizontal green time 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛, it grants the right-of-way to the horizontal direction; otherwise, it grants it to the vertical direction. Direction = {Horizontal, if 𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠 < 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 Vertical, if 𝑡𝑝𝑜𝑠 ≥ 𝑇𝐻_𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑒𝑛 (3 − 13) The parameters of this controller will be systematically optimized in the experimental design of Section 3.5.3 to find its best performance configuration. 3.3.2 Priority-Based Decentralized Strategy To establish a performance baseline, this study designed a priority -based decentralized strategy. This strategy can also be viewed as a “No -Central-Controller” scenario, intended to simulate an environment without any central traffic coordination mechanism. In this setting, the right-of-way at intersections is determined entirely by the robots themselves based on a simple, predefined set of priority rules. This strategy represents an important performance floor, used to measure the net benefit of any centralized control measure.

chunks.text: Design Principles and Decision Logic When multiple robots have a potential conflict at an intersection, the system assigns a priority to each robot based on its current task state. The priority levels are defined in 35 the table below, with the core principle being that tasks directly related to order fulfillment (such as delivering a pod to a workstation) have higher priority. Table 3.3.1 Priority levels Robot State (current_state) Task Description Priority delivering_pod Delivering pod to picking station Highest returning_pod Returning pod to storage area High taking_pod Going to storage area to pick up a pod Medium idle Idle or waiting Lowest At an intersection, the robot with the higher priority gets the right -of-way. This model, based entirely on individual greedy decisions, may perform well at low densities but is a source of high energy consumption and potential deadlock risk. 3.4 Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) Controller Design To apply the Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning framework to the traffic control problem of this study, we first establish the mapping of its core elements, which are detailed in the following subsections:  Agent: The traffic controller at each intersection.  Environment: The high-fidelity warehouse simulation system as described in Section 3.2.1. 36  State: The feature vector observed by the agent at the time of decision, its detailed composition is in Section 3.4.2.  Action: The discrete commands the agent can execute, its detailed composition is in Section 3.4.3.  Reward: a global fitness score calculated only at the end of an evaluation episode, its design philosophy and formula are detailed in Section 3.4.4.

chunks.section: 3. Energy Consumption Calculation Model
chunks.text: To cope with the high dynamics and complexity of traffic within RMFS and to learn to trade -off between multiple conflicting objectives like “throughput” and “energy consumption,” this study employs Neuroevolution Reinforcement Learning (NERL) to develop an intelligent traffic controller. Unlike traditional gradient -based reinforcement learning methods (like DQN), NERL optimizes directly in the parameter space of the policy.

chunks.section: 3. Energy Consumption Calculation Model
chunks.text: In this framework, the weights and biases 𝜃 of a neural network controller (i.e., a policy 𝜋𝜃) are treated as an individual’s Genotype. The algorithm searches for the policy network parameters 𝜃∗ that maximize the system’s long -term macroscopic benefits by performing “evaluation - selection-reproduction” evolutionary operations on a Population of many individuals. This method is more robust to sparse, delayed global reward signals and is naturally suited for large-scale parallel training [25] [29].

chunks.section: 3. Energy Consumption Calculation Model
chunks.text: This section will detail the core evolutionary process of the NERL controller, the state space, the action space, and the crucial design of the global reward function. 3.4.1 NERL Evolutionary Process The core process of NERL revolves around an “evaluation → selection → reproduction” evolutionary cycle, which iterates to improve the overall performance of 37 the population. Assume at generation 𝑔 there is a population 𝑃𝑔 = {𝜃1, 𝜃2, . . . , 𝜃𝑁} , containing 𝑁 individuals. 1. Evaluation: Each individual 𝜃𝑖 in the population is deployed in an independent simulation environment instance to run a full evaluation episode. During the episode, the policy 𝜋𝜃𝑖 makes all decisions independently. After the episode ends, a Fitness Score 𝐹(𝜃𝑖) is calculated for the individual based on the system’s macroscopic performance metrics (detailed in Section 3.4.4). 2.

chunks.section: 2. Selection: Based on the calculated fitness scores of all individuals, the algorithm
chunks.text: Selection: Based on the calculated fitness scores of all individuals, the algorithm selects high-performing individuals from the current population 𝑃𝑔 as Parents to provide genes for the next generation. This study uses Tournament Selection. 3.

chunks.section: 3. Reproduction: A new offspring population 𝑃𝑔+1 is generated by applying
chunks.text: Reproduction: A new offspring population 𝑃𝑔+1 is generated by applying genetic operations to the parents. The main operations include: o Elitism: To prevent losing the best solutions found during evolution, the top 𝑘 elite individuals with the highest fitness in each generation are directly and completely copied to the next generation’s population. o Crossover: Simulating biological reproduction, two individuals are selected from the parents, and their parameter vectors are mixed to create new offspring. o Mutation: A small random perturbation is applied to the parameters of the offspring individuals to maintain population diversity and avoid premature convergence. By iteratively executing the above cycle, the average fitness of the population will gradually increase, eventually converging to a high-performance policy network that can efficiently solve complex traffic control problems. 38 3.4.2 State Space Design The definition of the state space is a cornerstone of success in reinforcement learning. It must provide the agent with sufficient and meaningful information to make effective decisions. In the RMFS traffic control problem of this study, the state 𝑠𝑡 of any intersection at decision time 𝑡 is defined as a feature vector that comprehensively reflects its local traffic conditions while also considering the potential impact of neighboring and downstream intersections. Specifically, 𝑠𝑡 is a 17-dimensional continuous vector , which, after being processed by Adaptive Normalization, is divided into the following three parts: Table 3.4.1 State space State Type Dimension Feature Name Description Local State 1 Current Direction Indicates the current green light direction (horizontal/vertical) 1 Time Since Change The duration the current signal phase has been active 2 Queue Lengths (H/V) The number of queuing robots in each of the two directions 2 Priority Ratios (H/V) The proportion of robots in each queue performing high-priority tasks (e.g., delivering a pod) 2 Average Wait Times (H/V) The average waiting time of robots in each queue 39 State Type Dimension Feature Name Description Neighbor State 1 Neighbor Count The total number of adjacent intersections (1-4) 1 Total Neighbor Queue The total number of queuing robots at all neighboring intersections 1 Total Neighbor Priority Queue The total number of robots performing highpriority tasks at all neighboring intersections 1 Neighbor Priority Ratio The overall proportion of high-priority task robots at neighboring intersections 1 Neighbor Average Wait Time The average waiting time at all neighboring intersections 1 Neighbor Phase Distribution The proportion of neighboring intersections that are in horizontal and vertical green light phases, respectively 1 Neighbor Load Balance A metric for the disparity in queue lengths among neighboring intersections Note: Local state has 8 dimensions, neighbor state has 8 dimensions, totaling 16 dimensions, plus 1 dimension for global state (explained below), for a total of 17 dimensions. 3. Global State - 1 Dimension: A macroscopic indicator is introduced to help the agent align local decisions with overall system goals. * Picking Station Queue: The total queue length at the entrances of all picking stations, a key indicator of system-level bottlenecks.

chunks.section: 3. Global State - 1 Dimension: A macroscopic indicator is introduced to help the agent
chunks.text: 40 State Normalization Before feeding the state vector 𝑠𝑡 into the NERL model, this study employs an Adaptive Normalization technique. This technique dynamically tracks the running mean and standard deviation of each state feature during training and uses them to standardize the feature values, thereby ensuring the stability and efficiency of model training.

chunks.section: 3. Global State - 1 Dimension: A macroscopic indicator is introduced to help the agent
chunks.text: 3.4.3 Action Space Design This study designs a concise discrete action space 𝒜 for the DRL agent. At each decision point, the controller can choose an action 𝑎𝑡 ∈ 𝒜 from a set of 6 discrete actions. These actions cover basic traffic signal phase control and dynamic speed limits. • Basic Phase Control (3 actions): Keep Current Phase, Switch to Vertical Green, Switch to Horizontal Green. • Dynamic Speed Control (3 actions) : Remove Speed Limit (resume normal speed), Set Speed Limit to 50%, Set Speed Limit to 30%. All DRL controllers operate at a fixed decision interval of 𝑇decision = 10 ticks.

chunks.section: 3. Global State - 1 Dimension: A macroscopic indicator is introduced to help the agent
chunks.text: 3.4.4 Global Reward Function Design The reward function (often called the fitness function in evolutionary algorithms) is the core element that guides the agent’s behavior. To guide the NERL controller to learn complex trade-off strategies that are beneficial to the system’s long -term, macroscopic goals, this study designed a comprehensive Global Reward Function. In this model, the agent receives no immediate feedback throughout the evaluation episode. A single fitness score is calculated only at the end of the episode, based on the final ov erall performance of the system. 41 The design of this function incorporates established principles from the field of multi-objective optimization [30] and includes customized penalty terms (such as a longtail delay penalty) tailored to the unique challenges of the RMFS scenario in this study, to more comprehensively capture the system’s overall performance.

chunks.section: 3. Global State - 1 Dimension: A macroscopic indicator is introduced to help the agent
chunks.text: Its core formula is defined as follows: Fitness = (𝑁orders ⋅ 𝑤orders) − (𝐸total ⋅ 𝑤energy) − ∑ ( 𝑖∈𝑃 𝜆𝑖 ⋅ Penalty𝑖) (3 − 14) where 𝑁orders is the total number of completed orders, 𝐸total is the total energy consumption, and 𝑤orders and 𝑤energy are their corresponding weights. ∑(𝜆𝑖 ⋅ Penalty𝑖) is a series of weighted penalty terms used to penalize undesirable system behaviors. Specifically, the penalty term 𝑃 includes the following key parts: • Maximum Wait Time Penalty (𝑃wait): Penalizes the maximum robot waiting time that occurred throughout the simulation to encourage fairness and prevent individual robots from starving. • Average Wait Time Penalty (𝑃avg wait): Penalizes the average time of all waiting events to improve overall traffic fluidity. • Stop-and-Go Penalty (𝑃sg): Penalizes the total number of stop -and-go events in the system to encourage smooth traffic flow and indirectly reduce energy consumption. • Underutilization Penalty ( 𝑃util ): Penalizes situations where the average robot utilization falls below a certain reference value to encourage the system to maintain high operational efficiency. • Long-Tail Delay Penalty ( 𝑃tail ): Penalizes high -percentile waiting times (e.g., P95/P99) to specifically address and improve the worst experiences in the system. 42 All penalty terms are normalized based on a preset threshold before calculation, constraining them to the [0, 1] interval to ensure that penalties of different scales can be stably combined. This multi -objective, penalty -normalization-based fitness function design aims to guide the evolutionary process to find a comprehensively optimal solution that is not only high-throughput but also energy-efficient and highly stable. It is important to emphasize that the effectiveness of this reward function is not proven through theoretical derivation but will be empirically validated by the experimental results in Chapter 4. If the NERL controller trained based on this function can demonstrate the expected intelligent trade-off behavior between multiple conflicting objectives in the final performance evaluation, then this design can be considered successful. 3.5 Experimental Design and Evaluation Process To rigorously answer the research questions posed in the introduction, this study designed a systematic three -phase experimental process. chunks.text: 3.6.1 Training Process The training of NERL is a generation-iterative, off-policy learning process. A single complete training experiment follows this procedure: 1. Initialization: 47 a. An instance of NEController is created according to the hyperparameters described in Section 3.6.2. b. The controller randomly initializes a population of 30 network individuals. 2.

chunks.section: 2. Evolutionary Loop:
chunks.text: Evolutionary Loop: a. An evolution is started for 20 generations. b. In each generation g: i. Parallel Evaluation: For the 30 individuals in the population, 30 independent simulation environments are launched. ii. Each individual runs a full evaluation episode of 25,000 ticks in its dedicated environment. To ensure consistency in learning objectives, all evaluations are conducted under a fixed order demand; however, a different random seed is used for each evaluation to change initial conditions (like Pod layout), thereby generating diverse, dynamic training scenarios for the controller through real-time interaction with the simulator. iii.

chunks.section: 2. Evolutionary Loop:
chunks.text: After the episode, the fitness score of the individual is calculated according to the global reward function defined in Section 3.4.4. iv. Evolutionary Operation : Once the fitness scores of all individuals are calculated, the controller performs a full evolutionary operation (selection, crossover, mutation) to generate a new offspring population. 3.

chunks.section: 3. Model Saving:
chunks.text: Model Saving: a. At the end of each generation, the algorithm saves the individual with the highest fitness in that generation as the best model of that generation. b. After the evolution of all generations is complete, the model with the 48 highest fitness score across all generations is selected as the final model for the final performance comparison in Section 3.5.4. 3.6.2 Neural Network Architecture The neural network used by the NERL controller in this study is a standard Feed - Forward Neural Network. To this end, this paper first established a standardized, medium -density warehouse simulation scenario.

According to the experimental results in Chapter 4, this study revealed a clear performance trade-off among the different strategies: The priority-based decentralized strategy established the upper limit for system throughput, with an order completion rate significantly higher than the other two controlled strategies. However, this high output came at the cost of substantial energy consumption, making it representative of a “high-throughput, high-energy” approach. 69  The NERL strategy demonstrated a commanding advantage in energy efficiency, with its energy per order being statistically significantly lower than both baseline strategies. However, this significant energy saving was achieved by sacrificing some system throughput, as its c ompletion rate was significantly lower than the decentralized strategy.  The optimized Time-Based strategy’s performance on various metrics fell between the other two, offering a relatively balanced but non-optimal solution. Overall, the core finding of this study is that the NERL controller did not surpass traditional methods on all metrics.

chunks.text: 5.3 Research Limitations To ensure the focus and depth of this study, the applicability of its conclusions is also limited by its research boundaries. Acknowledging these limitations will help in objectively understanding the contributions of this study and will point the way for future research. 71 • Limitation in Algorithm Breadth: The core of this study was to compare three different control “philosophies,” not to conduct a large -scale performance competition of algorithms.

chunks.text: Therefore, to deeply analyze the potential of NERL in trade-off learning, the research scope did not include a horizontal performance comparison of various deep reinforcement learning algorithms (such as DQN, A3C, etc.). • Limitation in Scenario Generalizability: All conclusions of this study are based on a specific, medium -density warehouse scenario. Although the scenario was designed to be representative, whether the findings of this study, especially regarding the performance ranking and energy -saving potentia l of different strategies, can be directly generalized to higher or lower density, or to warehouse environments with different physical layouts, remains an open question that requires further empirical research. • Independence of Path Planning: This study assumed that the global paths of all robots were pre-determined by an independent A* algorithm. The core focus was on local conflict coordination at the intersection level and did not involve the possibility of jointly optimizing traffic control with global path planning. • Fixity of Hyperparameters : To ensure consistency in comparison, this study used a fixed set of hyperparameter configurations for the NERL controller. The study did not conduct systematic hyperparameter tuning or ablation studies, so it cannot be claimed that the current configuration is the global optimum. 5.4 Future Work Based on the findings and existing limitations of this study, future research can be deepened and expanded in the following directions: 72 1.

chunks.text: Expanding Training Scale to Explore Performance Limits : Although the performance trend line of the NERL training in this study showed an upward trend after 20 generations, it had not yet reached a fully converged stable state. Therefore, a direct and valuable future research direction is to significantly extend the number of training generations (e.g., to 50 or 100 generations) with more powerful computational resources. This would help to more fully explore the upper potential of the NERL model and could verify whether longer training can lead the agent to find a more advantageous Pareto Optimal front [30] in the “throughput-energy” trade-off space. 2. Cross-Scenario Generalization Ability Verification: To more comprehensively evaluate the robustness of the NERL controller, future research could deploy the optimal model trained in this study directly into warehouse environments with different robot densities (higher or lower) and different physical layouts for “Zeroshot” or “Fine -tuning” tests. This would allow for a deeper evaluation of its policy’s generalization ability and reveal potential weaknesses of the current model in adapting to new environments. 3. Joint Optimization of Traffic Control and Global Path Planning : This study treated path planning and traffic control as two separate modules. However, in the real world, the two are highly coupled. Future research could explore a more ambitious framework, for example, by feeding the congestion level of intersections as a dynamic cost back to the upstream global path planner, thereby constructing a multi-agent learning system that can achieve “path planning-traffic control” joint optimization. 4.
